Duration: ~48 minutes

summary: Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and fallback policies for Fortuna's planned LLM features. Key concerns: multi-region failover, model fallbacks to cheaper/compatible variants, SLA expectations for hosted vs dedicated vs private, and security/compliance (audit logs, KMS, SSO). Agreed next steps: send security pack, benchmark sheet, gather traffic sample, schedule POC scoping.

Model fallback strategies and quality tradeoffs
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for incident tolerance
Security controls: audit logs, KMS, SSO/SAML, SOC2
questions: What is Redwood's expected RTO/RPO for hosted endpoints?
How are fallbacks chosen automatically, and can we pin model variants?
Does Dedicated provide guaranteed cross-region capacity or do we need Private for strict residency?
How is KV cache and prefix caching handled across regions?
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, well kick off, I'm Maya from Redwood, with Liam our SE. Quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Aisha here, Head of Platform at Fortuna, we own infra for new LLM features. Carlos and Sophie are with me.
[00:18] Carlos Moreno: Carlos, SRE.
[00:22] Sophie Lee: Sophie, PM working on recommendations flow.
[00:26] Maya Chen: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand reliability and incident tolerance needs: multi-region failover, fallbacks, SLAs, and which deployment mode you're leaning toward.
[00:38] Sophie Lee: To give context, our roadmap has two services: real-time chat for support and a nightly batch reranking job. The realtime is sensitive to latency, we want p95 < 150ms and p99 < 350ms if possible.
[00:52] Liam Patel: Got it. Are you currently using any hosted LLM providers?
[00:57] Aisha Rahman: We're piloting with two vendors, and some self-hosted experiments. Latency varies and we've had incidents where a region had degraded throughput. We're evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[01:10] Maya Chen: Common. For incident tolerance, Redwood supports smart routing and multi-region fallbacks: policy-based routing, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to compatible model variants when a region or model is degraded.
[01:26] Carlos Moreno: How do you detect degradation? Is it health probes, queue depth, or backend metrics? We need deterministic failovers.
[01:34] Liam Patel: We ingest latency and error rate metrics at the control plane. Policy thresholds (e.g., sustained p99 > target or error rate spike) trigger circuit-breakers and route traffic to healthy pools or a secondary region. Detection is metric-driven, you can tweak thresholds.
[01:48] Carlos Moreno: And if the secondary region has a slightly different model (quantized or smaller), how do you handle output quality?
[01:55] Liam Patel: Good question. We recommend model variants matrix: primary high-capacity model for low latency and high quality, fallback to quantized or smaller variants with a known quality delta. Redwood's routing can be quality-aware: you set acceptable degradation and we only failover to variants that meet that bar. We also support shadowing and A/B canaries to measure impact before full cutover.
[02:14] Sophie Lee: Can we pin models per route? For compliance we sometimes need to pin a version.
[02:19] Maya Chen: Yes, you can pin model versions and set rollout policies per route. That works across Hosted and Dedicated. Private gives you full control of underlying infra.
[02:27] Aisha Rahman: SLA-wise, what's Redwood's guarantee for Hosted? We need to present to execs.
[02:32] Maya Chen: Hosted has tiered SLAs—standard is 99.5% monthly availability, enterprise tiers with dedicated commitments can go higher. Dedicated reserved capacity gives you more predictable throughput and we can negotiate latency/availability SLOs with capacity commitments. Private is where you control everything and can meet strict residency/SLA through an enterprise agreement. I'll send the SLA doc.
[02:50] Carlos Moreno: On multi-region, if a primary region goes down, is there a global control plane decision or is it DNS based? We worry about DNS TTLs and slow DNS failover.
[02:59] Liam Patel: Routing is control-plane driven with direct routing to region endpoints; we prefer not to rely on DNS alone. In-hosted mode we push routing changes within seconds internally. For Dedicated we can set up cross-region peering and automated failover pipelines. For Private deployments we provide the control plane API and ops runbooks.
[03:15] Carlos Moreno: What about KV cache invalidation when failing over? Our stateful sessions matter.
[03:20] Liam Patel: We support prefix/KV cache replication and regional sticky sessions. For strict state we recommend session affinity or a global cache layer; otherwise upon failover we have a degraded but safe path: cache miss -> recompute. We can also sync hot prefixes across two regions for small window RTO.
[03:36] Sophie Lee: Is there any manual playbook? We need runbooks to be able to override auto-failover.
[03:41] Maya Chen: Absolutely. There are manual overrides, mute/force routes, and a canary gating UI in Redwood Console. We also provide audit logs for every routing decision.
[03:50] Aisha Rahman: How do you do degradation gracefully? If model quality drops we prefer to throttle or return a short fallback message rather than produce low-quality output.
[03:57] Liam Patel: You can configure policies: degrade to 'safe mode' responses, route to a smaller model with a disclaimer, or use cached responses for high-traffic prompts. Throttling and queueing policies can also be tuned per route.
[04:10] Carlos Moreno: Security: we need KMS integration, audit logs, SSO, and SOC2 stuff. Also data residency for EU customers.
[04:18] Maya Chen: We support KMS/HSM, full audit logs, RBAC, and SAML/SSO. Hosted can meet many compliance needs; for strict residency or air-gapped requirements we recommend Private. I'll attach the security pack and SOC2 report.
[04:31] Aisha Rahman: Great. On cost, Dedicated seems attractive but how does cost scale if we need cross-region standby capacity?
[04:38] Liam Patel: You can provision dedicated pools per region with autoscaling policies and burst options. Some customers keep a smaller warm standby region to reduce cost and use automated scaling during failover. Redwood Optimize will give quantization and batching recommendations to reduce per-token cost.
[04:55] Sophie Lee: For the POC, we want to test a real failover scenario with our traffic. Can Redwood help simulate region failure and fallback?
[05:01] Liam Patel: Yes, during POC we run chaos tests: simulated region outage, model degradation, and observe routing and latency. We'll include scripts and expected metrics.
[05:10] Carlos Moreno: How is observability surfaced? We need token-level latency, per-route p95/p99, and traces.
[05:16] Maya Chen: Console shows per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, tracing hooks, and integration with Datadog/Prometheus. We'll provide a sample dashboard and metrics mapping.
[05:26] Aisha Rahman: Any known gotchas with multi-region? Cross-region data egress, replication delays, and model artifacts syncing come to mind.
[05:33] Liam Patel: Exactly—model weights syncing and cache warming are the main ones. We recommend pre-warming fallback variants in the standby region and keeping model artifacts in object storage with fast regional replication.
[05:45] Sophie Lee: Can you do model translation between variants automatically or do we have to create separate fine-tuned variants?
[05:51] Liam Patel: You manage model variants; Redwood can help with conversion (quantization) and maintain compatibility. Auto-translation isn't magic—there's an ops step. We'll share best-practices.
[05:59] Aisha Rahman: If we run into an incident and need egress logs for an audit, how fast can Redwood deliver?
[06:05] Maya Chen: Audit logs are retained per plan — enterprise plans have extended retention and we can push logs to your S3 or SIEM. Delivery SLA for logs is part of the contract.
[06:15] Carlos Moreno: OK next steps would be: get the security pack, see benchmarks, and scope a POC where we run a simulated failover.
[06:22] Maya Chen: Agreed. Liam and I will compile items. We'll also ask you to share two weeks of anonymized request samples and your top-5 prompts so we can run realistic benches.
[06:33] Sophie Lee: We'll do that. Also we want a pricing delta for adding standby region capacity for Dedicated.
[06:38] Maya Chen: We'll include ballpark estimates in the pricing doc.
[06:42] Aisha Rahman: Perfect. Thank you both.
[06:45] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the security pack and benchmark spreadsheet. 
[06:50] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcribed text contains occasional mis-hearings; references: security pack link (sent): https://redwood.example.com/security-pack, benchmark template: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/fortuna-template, POC scoping doc placeholder.
